{{Short description|Type of roulette curve}}

[[Image:EpitrochoidIn1.gif|right|thumb|300px|Construction of the limaçon {{math|1=r = 2 + cos(&pi; – &theta;)}} with [[polar coordinates]]' origin at {{math|1=(''x'', ''y'') = ({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0)}}]]

In [[geometry]], a '''limaçon''' or '''limacon''' ({{IPA|fr|limasɔ̃|link=yes}}), also known as a '''limaçon of Pascal''' or '''Pascal's Snail''', is defined as a [[roulette (curve)|roulette curve]] formed by the path of a [[Point (geometry)|point]] fixed to a [[circle]] when that circle [[Rolling|rolls]] around the outside of a circle of equal radius. It can also be defined as the roulette formed when a circle rolls around a circle with half its radius so that the smaller circle is inside the larger circle. Thus, they belong to the family of curves called [[centered trochoid]]s; more specifically, they are [[epitrochoid]]s. The '''[[cardioid]]''' is the special case in which the point generating the roulette lies on the rolling circle; the resulting curve has a [[cusp (singularity)|cusp]].

Depending on the position of the point generating the curve, it may have inner and outer loops (giving the family its name),  it may be [[heart (symbol)|heart]]-shaped, or it may be oval.

A limaçon is a [[circular algebraic curve|bicircular]] rational plane [[algebraic curve]] of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] 4.

==History==
The earliest formal research on limaçons is generally attributed to [[Étienne Pascal]], father of [[Blaise Pascal]]. However, some insightful investigations regarding them had been undertaken earlier by the [[Germany|German]] [[Renaissance]] artist [[Albrecht Dürer]]. Dürer's ''Underweysung der Messung (Instruction in Measurement)'' contains specific geometric methods for producing limaçons. The curve was named by [[Gilles de Roberval]] when he used it as an example for finding tangent lines, deriving the word from the latin ''limax'': snail.

==Equations==
[[Image:Limacons.svg|right|thumb|500px|Three limaçons: dimpled, with cusp (a [[cardioid]]), and looped. Not shown: the [[Convex set|convex]] limaçon]]The equation (up to translation and rotation) of a limaçon in [[polar coordinates]] has the form

:<math>r = b + a \cos \theta.</math>

This can be converted to [[Cartesian coordinate]]s by multiplying by ''r'' (thus introducing a point at the origin which in some cases is spurious), and substituting <math>r^2 = x^2+y^2</math> and <math>r \cos \theta = x</math> to obtain<ref name=Lawrence>{{cite book | author=J. Dennis Lawrence | title=A catalog of special plane curves | publisher=Dover Publications | year=1972 | isbn=0-486-60288-5 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/catalogofspecial00lawr/page/113 113–118] | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/catalogofspecial00lawr/page/113 }}</ref>

:<math>\left(x^2 + y^2 - ax\right)^2 = b^2\left(x^2 + y^2\right).</math>

Applying the parametric form of the polar to Cartesian conversion, we also have<ref name=Weisstein>[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Limacon.html Weisstein, Eric W. "Limaçon." From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource.]</ref>

:<math>x = (b + a\cos \theta)\cos \theta = {a\over 2} + b \cos \theta + {a\over 2} \cos 2 \theta,</math>
:<math>y = (b + a\cos \theta)\sin \theta = b \sin \theta + {a\over 2} \sin 2 \theta;</math>

while setting

:<math>z = x + i y = ( b + a \cos \theta )( \cos \theta + i \sin \theta )</math>

yields this parameterization as a curve in the [[complex plane]]:

:<math>z = {a \over 2} + b e^{i\theta} + {a\over 2} e^{2i\theta}.</math>

If we were to shift horizontally by <math display="inline">-\frac{1}{2}a</math>, i.e.,

:<math>z = b e^{it} + {a \over 2} e^{2it}</math>,

we would, by changing the location of the origin, convert to the usual form of the equation of a centered trochoid. Note the change of independent variable at this point to make it clear that we are no longer using the default polar coordinate parameterization <math>\theta = \arg z</math>.

===Special cases===
In the special case <math>a = b</math>, the polar equation is

:<math>r = b(1 + \cos \theta) = 2b\cos^2 \frac{\theta}{2}</math> 

or 

:<math>r^{1 \over 2} = (2b)^{1 \over 2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2},</math> 

making it a member of the [[sinusoidal spiral]] family of curves. This curve is the [[cardioid]].

In the special case <math>a = 2b</math>, the centered trochoid form of the equation becomes

:<math>z = b \left(e^{it} + e^{2it}\right) = b e^{3it\over 2} \left(e^{it\over 2} + e^{-it\over 2}\right) = 2b  e^{3it\over 2} \cos{t \over 2},</math>

or, in polar coordinates,

:<math>r = 2b\cos{\theta \over 3}</math>

making it a member of the [[Rose (mathematics)|rose]] family of curves. This curve is a [[trisectrix]], and is sometimes called the [[limaçon trisectrix]].

==Form==
When <math>b > a</math>, the limaçon is a simple closed curve. However, the origin satisfies the Cartesian equation given above, so the graph of this equation has an [[acnode]] or isolated point.

When <math>b > 2a</math>, the area bounded by the curve is convex, and when <math>a < b < 2a</math>, the curve has an indentation bounded by two [[inflection point]]s. At <math>b = 2a</math>, the point <math>(-a, 0)</math> is a point of 0 [[curvature]].

As <math>b</math> is decreased relative to <math>a</math>, the indentation becomes more pronounced until, at <math>b = a</math>, the curve becomes a cardioid, and the indentation becomes a [[cusp (singularity)|cusp]]. For <math>0 < b < a</math>, the cusp expands to an inner loop, and the curve crosses itself at the origin. As <math>b</math> approaches 0, the loop fills up the outer curve and, in the limit, the limaçon becomes a circle traversed twice.

==Measurement==
The area enclosed by the limaçon <math>r = b + a \cos \theta</math> is <math display="inline">\left(b^2 + {{a^2} \over 2}\right)\pi</math>. When <math>b < a</math> this counts the area enclosed by the inner loop twice. In this case the curve crosses the origin at angles <math display="inline">\pi \pm \arccos {b \over a}</math>, the area enclosed by the inner loop is

:<math> \left (b^2 + {{a^2}\over 2} \right )\arccos {b \over a} - {3\over 2} b \sqrt{a^2 - b^2},</math> 

the area enclosed by the outer loop is 

:<math> \left(b^2 + {{a^2}\over 2} \right ) \left (\pi - \arccos {b \over a} \right ) + {3\over 2} b \sqrt{a^2 -b^2},</math> 

and the area between the loops is 

:<math> \left (b^2 + {{a^2}\over 2} \right ) \left (\pi - 2\arccos {b \over a} \right ) + 3b \sqrt{a^2 -b^2}.</math><ref name=Lawrence/>

The circumference of the limaçon is given by a [[Elliptic Integral|complete elliptic integral of the second kind]]:

:<math> 4(a + b)E\left({{2\sqrt{ab}} \over a + b}\right).</math>

==Relation to other curves==
* Let <math>P</math> be a point and <math>C</math> be a circle whose center is not <math>P</math>. Then the envelope of those circles whose center lies on <math>C</math> and that pass through <math>P</math> is a limaçon.
[[Image:PedalCurve2.gif|500px|right|thumb|Limaçon — [[pedal curve]] of a [[circle]]]]

* A [[Pedal curve|pedal]] of a [[circle]] is a limaçon. In fact, the pedal with respect to the origin of the circle with radius <math>b</math> and center <math>(a, 0)</math> has polar equation <math>r = b + a \cos \theta</math>.

* The [[Inversive geometry#Inversion of an algebraic curve|inverse]] with respect to the unit circle of <math>r = b + a \cos \theta</math> is 

::<math>r = {1 \over {b + a \cos \theta}}</math> 

:which is the equation of a [[conic section]] with eccentricity <math>\tfrac{a}{b}</math> and focus at the origin. Thus a limaçon can be defined as the inverse of a conic where the center of inversion is one of the foci. If the conic is a parabola then the inverse will be a cardioid, if the conic is a hyperbola then the corresponding limaçon will have an inner loop, and if the conic is an ellipse then the corresponding limaçon will have no loop.

* The [[conchoid (mathematics)|conchoid]] of a circle with respect to a point on the circle is a limaçon.

* A particular special case of a [[Cartesian oval]] is a limaçon.<ref>{{MacTutor|class= Curves|id= Cartesian|title=Cartesian Oval}}</ref>
